items.title: The Tide Finally Turned Against the Depredations of the Trump II Presidency
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
We, the lucky ones, emerged this week from one of the darkest stretches in American history. The jubilation, the relief, the exhilaration are heartfelt and genuine and real and understandable. But not everyone who began this arduous journey with us was still around to celebrate its climactic conclusion.

Over the past 22 months, there have been innumerable tangible real world victims of the Trump II rampage: the millions of abandoned beneficiaries of USAID; the sick and dying betrayed by MAHA’s perverse notions of public health; the countless families ripped apart by indiscriminate mass deportation; the hundreds of immigrants dumped in countries with which they had no prior connection; the forgotten souls shipped off to foreign gulags; Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

There is no minimizing or excusing it. What they have lost is not recoverable. There is no making them whole again.

The COVID pandemic taught those of us who didn’t already know it the cruel lesson of how quickly humans forget and move on. Down deep, it may be a biological imperative, but we have refined it with a culture of short attention spans, a cultivated urgency to be always looking ahead, and an infinite ability to tell ourselves soothing and self-congratulatory stories about our own greatness.

Moments in history like these, when America redeems her lost promise, are uplifting and tantalizing with possibility — for those who survived what came before. The toils of slavery, the carnage of a civil war, the dehumanization of Jim Crow exacted extreme tolls in human misery and suffering, and the harrowing accounts of all but a very few individual victims are lost to history. There were in fact few happy endings.

In a culture that worships heroes, our stories are so full of them that I grew up internalizing that heroes were everywhere in every story and that all of us should be poised to be heroes in our own stories. It was only during COVID and the depredations of the Trump era that I finally came to see how rare heroes actually are and to understand that we are obsessed with heroes and with neat tidy Hollywood endings precisely because they are so rare in real life.

The heroes of the past nearly two years are not the people you’ve seen on TV or the pundits you’ve read or those who have delivered the loudest smackdowns of Trump. They weren’t posturing or preening. They were doing thankless tedious work that is neither glamorous nor lucrative. The work of democracy is boring, bureaucratic, and procedural — but essential all the same.

The heroes have been court staffs, paralegals, clerks, and junior associates working all night in emergency proceedings. They’ve been public interest lawyers, solo immigration attorneys, and immigrant advocates who were already familiar with the Kafkaesque immigration system even before Trump returned to office and made it infinitely worse.

Widening the circle, they’ve been health care providers, NGO workers, and arts administrators tirelessly endeavoring to preserve public services while fending off attacks. They’ve been parents struggling to provide normal childhoods to children who have been targeted because they’re brown or trans or disabled.

We, too, will move on in due course. But I didn’t want to do it yet without acknowledging who and what we’ve lost along the way.

I am deeply grateful that you have stuck with Morning Memo over the past two years. I did not make it easy on you.

I vowed not to sugarcoat the reality of Trump II but to chronicle it unstintingly. When things were at their most bewildering and hard to categorize in familiar ways, I threw enormous amounts of information at you. It was often raw and unsorted as I felt my way towards making sense of it all.

I refused, maybe stubbornly, to cast events in hopeful or optimistic terms unless they truly deserved it. I didn’t try to stuff events into artificial framings that fed the earnest desire for comeuppance, the hero’s revenge, or the villain’s fall.

It was a hard slog for readers. Many of you told me so. Morning Memo was difficult to read, hard to stomach, and relentless day after day for months on end.

Politics was grim. People wanted to avert their eyes. Many tuned politics outs or hit pause.

After a dramatic upswing in readership during the initial wave of Trump II atrocities in February and March 2025, it became hard to grow the audience for Morning Memo. The audience plateaued, but it didn’t shrink.

I feel a fierce pride in you for riding it out with me.

Trump II is not over yet. But we’ve clearly entered a new phase, with dramatically different power dynamics and a chance finally to move from a defensive crouch trying to protect what precious ground could be saved to taking the offensive and beginning to reclaim vast areas of American public life.

I look forward to navigating this next phase with you.

The Remaining Senate Races Edge Blue

: Scott Colom (D) has widened his lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R). The latest AP tally has him up by 1,936 votes, as the legal fight over the super-close election begins to take shape.

: The NYT projects that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) is likely to sustain her narrow lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) even if she falls short of an outright majority and the election is decided on ranked choice. Meanwhile, President Trump wildly claimed that Sullivan should declare the winner.

Straight Into My Veins: Southern Gains

  • WSJ: The Red Wall Falls: Democrats Shatter Decades of GOP Dominance Across the South

Straight Into My Veins: Texas Sweep

  • Politico: Democratic Attorneys General Just Took Texas Off the Board: “We took the head of the snake.”

  • Texas Tribune: How schools could change for millions of students.

  • Politico: How Dems’ sweep in Texas blows up the 2028 map.

”I am not going to answer that question because that is a stupid question.”—longtime voter fraud bamboozler and election denier Cleta Mitchell, when asked by the NYT if she would join with President Trump in accepting the results of the 2026 election

Sher-ROD! I Will Never Unhear This ...

Trump DOJ Watch: Personnel Shuffle Edition

Some notable departures post-election from the Trump DOJ:

  • Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who was overseeing the bogus investigation of the so-called “grand conspiracy” against Trump by the Deep State

  • Henry C. Whitaker, counselor to the attorney general, who among other things was handling the appeals in the James Comey and Letitia James prosecutions.

Be careful: No clear through line connects all of these departures, and there are often post-election personnel shuffles.

A Grim But Essential Read

Perhaps as a reminder that our struggles to preserve democracy have been more modest than we might like to admit: An incredible survival tale of one Ukrainian infantryman hunkered down alone on the front line against Russia as his body slowly disintegrated.

items.title: Has The Political Press Still Learned Nothing After a Decade of Trump?
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
It’s been a jangly 36 hours watching America rise up against a wannabe authoritarian while the political press resorts to the same old tired tropes as if it were hungry to go back to the pre-Trump days or pretend they never happened.

The U.S. press does a fine job covering democratic uprisings in foreign countries, but struggles mightily to cover them here at home.

While the midterm elections here fit neatly into a pattern of right-wing defeats in the past few weeks in Serbia and Brazil, the mainstream media here — even after a decade — is still grasping to employ suitable language for the current authoritarian moment in the United States.

The failures of the post-election news coverage mostly revolve around the embrace of worn-out horse-race campaign coverage and quickie post-election analysis in which losers lose because they’re idiots, and winners win because they’re geniuses.

The inability to grapple open and honestly with the Christian nationalist neo-fascism of the Trump II presidency continues to bedevil domestic political coverage. In one of its post-election analyses, the NYT allowed that it was “a decisive rebuke to President Trump and his aggressive, often chaotic second-term agenda.”

“Aggressive and often chaotic” are doing an awful lot of work there, as if the second term was an emotionally dis-regulated child with poorly medicated ADHD.

Contrast that with the NYT’s description of Viktor Orban’s election defeat in April, which it credited with “breaking the momentum of a global nationalist revival promoted by President Trump.” The Hungarian election, it reported, was a “showdown between friends and foes of liberal democracy.”

The coverage of an anodyne tweet by Vice President JD Vance yesterday captured the hunger of the political press to return to the coverage of old. Vance repeated what President Trump had already said — and what he would reaffirm after being asked about Vance’s tweet: that the Iran War cost them the election.

Yet that somehow that become evidence of a dramatic break between Vance and Trump — even though Vance conceded little, took blame for nothing, and whitewashed the entire rest of the “aggressive, often chaotic second-term agenda,” to borrow a phrase. Perhaps the Vance team self-servingly nudged reporters toward that interpretation, as the publication of a “tick-tock” of the tweet by Politico might suggest.

Blaming the Iran War is poised to become this cycle’s overly simplistic post-election narrative device. It offends almost no one, absolves the rest of the Trump II depredations, and misses its own anti-democratic origins.

We’re at risk of having the blue wave chalked up merely to the pocketbook impacts of the Iran War and the Trump tariffs without connecting either of them to the underlying authoritarianism involved.

The Iran War and the Trump tariffs, many of which (though not all) were struck down by the Supreme Court, were unilateral and illegal acts by the executive branch.

Trump sidelined Congress in violation of the constitutional order. These weren’t merely bad or poorly executed policies. The founders knew from experience that this is the folly you get from giving too much power to one man.

The notion that Republicans were victimized by Trump’s political “missteps” and “miscalculations” necessarily supposes that his rogue anti-democratic presidency is somehow disconnected from the horrible outcomes it produces. It also unwittingly implies that if the outcomes had been good, the means would have been fine.

It’s the Economy AND Corruption, Stupid

More Fun With Midterms Data

An assortment of interesting data points:

  • “Republicans have not won a House of Representatives ‌seat in ⁠a district that Trump carried by less than 11 percentage points two years ago. … Democrats have won four seats that Trump carried by more than 15 percentage points.”—

  • “Of about 3,000 counties where at least half the expected vote for the House has been tallied, all but about 170 saw Republican candidates run behind President Trump’s 2024 margin against Kamala Harris. The median county shifted about 11 percentage points toward the Democrats.”—

  • “Republicans are only on track to flip one House seat, in Maine, that they didn’t redraw last year.”—

Quote of the Day: Texas Edition

“Calling it a dummymander is generous. This was more like moron-mandering. We went for five seats, won none, killed an incumbent, and handed Democrats a reason to turn out. Was living with Henry Cuellar really that hard?”—an anonymous Texas GOP strategist whom Politico described as “frustrated”

Chart of the Day: Texas Edition

Democrats swept every demographic and geographic subgroup, according to the Times Voter Trends, except these (with the margin for Republicans):

    Impact on the New Congress

    Despite the Supreme Court’s decision in and subsequent aggressive Republican mid-decade redistricting to eliminate Black majority-minority districts, the impact on the new Congress is more nuanced than I might have expected.

    • A total of 8 seats are going from Black to non-Black members, but four of those were held by Black Republicans, three of whom ran for higher office.

    • A total of 6 seats are going from non-Black to Black members.

    • Two Black members targeted by the GOP mid-decade redistricting scheme appear likely to survive: Shomari Figures (D-AL) and Don Davis (D-NC).

    The blue wave unquestionably muted the effects of … and I can’t emphasize this enough … .

    Before anyone interprets these numbers as minimizing what’s happened to Black voter representation in the South, was always understood to have more dramatic effects on state and local representation than on Congress. One of its biggest knock-on effects is to deprive Black candidates of access to the lower rungs of the political ladder that they can use to reach Congress.

    It’s also important to remember that the Voting Rights Act was about empowering Black , not Black candidates — so diversity among electeds is only a rough proxy for Black political power.

    This all comes against the backdrop of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) being poised to become the first Black speaker of the House and the addition of Juliana Stratton (D-IL) giving the Senate a record number of six Black senators, with a seventh if Scott Colom (D) wins in Mississippi.

    Mike Johnson Won’t Return as GOP Leader

    Outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) won’t seek to return as the House GOP leader in the next Congress, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise (LA) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (OH) to duke it out.

    This WaPo headline is a false dichotomy often used to manufacture storylines in political coverage: “Democrats face a choice on Trump come January: Confrontation or compromise.”

    Confrontation v. compromise is as flat, reductive, and imprecise as most of the dreary analysis of the moderate v. progressive fault line within the Democratic Party. There is understandable hunger for the prototypical Democratic officeholder to be more robust, combative, and decisive; but this kind of thin analysis sets up an easy gotcha for subsequent coverage that doesn’t reflect the strength of Democrats’ new majorities on the Hill.

    The reality is Democrats do not face a stark choice between confrontation and compromise. The can do both or either or neither. They get to pick when and where to fight their battles. They get to decide which hills to die on. They are in the driver’s seat.

    Besieged District Courts Get Relief

    Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck, on the critical relief that a Democratic Congress can provide federal district courts:

    [T]he district courts have been under siege—even as they have been instrumental in standing up for the rule of law by fighting a classic rear-guard action. Unlike Blanche, they haven’t been trying to win a “war,” but rather just trying to hold the line in the hope that reinforcements would eventually be on their way.

    Thanks to Tuesday’s election results, those reinforcements are coming—in the form of a House of Representatives and Senate that will be just as interested in checking the executive branch …

    Races to Watch: Schadenfreude Edition

    Obviously all eyes remain on the Mississippi and Alaska Senate races, which still hang in the balance, but longtime TPM readers will want to keep an eye on two House races that remain too close to call:

    : Republican Rep. , 48%, is trailing Democrat Eileen Laubacher, 48.7%, with 93% of the votes counted. Boebert, first elected to Congress in 2020, has been the archetypical MAGA-era GOP House member: a transgressive, attention-seeking wild child with a messy personal life.

    : Rep. (R) is trailing by 280 votes against Democrat Victoria Broderick, with 99% of the votes counted. DesJarlais predates the Trump era, having arrived in the Tea Party wave of 2010. He has persisted, shall we say, despite his own personal messiness being exposed earlier in his congressional career.

items.title: A Glorious Night: Bask in America’s Own Redemption
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.

Behold the New U.S. Political Map

Wow. It’s impossible to get my head around the sweeping changes to the map coming out of last night. It’s going to take few days to process it all. Just wow.

The final totals in the House and Senate aren’t in yet and might not be known for several more days, but as it stands now, the outcome leaves Democrats with congressional majorities that look a lot like what they won in the 2008 election that swept Barack Obama into office in the aftermath of another unpopular Middle East war.

The NYT is projecting that Democrats will wind up with 55 Senate seats and 258 seats in the House. After the 2008 election, Democrats had 56 Senate seats and 257 House seats. (This is never a perfect comparison because the numbers fluctuate throughout each Congress, with deaths, party switches, etc.) But that only tells part of the story.

What about the sheer gain of 10 Senate seats? Republicans picked up 10 Senate seats in the 1994 election, but Democrats haven’t added that many seats since they picked up 15 seats in the 1958 election, the beginning of a Democratic Senate majority that would last until the 1980 election.

And the gain of 42 House seats? You don’t have to go that far back: Democrats picked up 41 seats in the 2020 election.

But matching the size of Democratic majority after 2008 — ±257 seats — means equalling the high water mark for Democrats since the 1994 election, the seminal election which ended their 42-year House majority. To put it in the context of our current politics, this Democratic majority will be significantly bigger than any recent Republican majority. The GOP high water mark in the House in the modern era was 247 seats after the 2014 election.

With the results still coming in, this isn’t about pinpointing which records have been set yet, but just about giving you some sense of the historic comps.

Beyond the Senate and House, entire states turned completely blue, with statehouse trifectas (governor plus control of both legislative chambers) in:

Democrats broke statehouse trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. They will hold a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years.

  • : Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan

  • : Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia

  • Native American female governor: Deb Haaland in New Mexico

  • : Chris Pappas in New Hampshire

Biggest Upset of the Night:

Biggest Wow of the Night: Texas

The dual toxicity of Donald Trump and Ken Paxton finally brought a blue wave to Texas that had been nearly 30 years in the making. Gone in one fell swoop are:

  • Attorney General Ken Paxton

The View from Across the Pond

  • BBC: Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump’s Republicans

  • The Independent: Trump told Americans to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot.’ They did — and voted against him

  • : Regardless of what happens, an amazing showing by Scott Colom.

  • : A lot still to be figured out, especially with ranked-choice voting.

From the GOP Insider Perspective …

The inside-the-beltway pubs framed last night’s result in GOP terms, as they usually do:

We’ve had some fluky elections in the past 20 years, where Republicans in particular have fielded bad candidates or where the timing of vacancies has created outlier results. But this was so broad-based that there was nothing fluky about it.

I look in particular at the Senate races across the South: South Carolina, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, and Louisiana. Even the losing Democratic candidates had remarkably strong performances. The groundswell was nationwide.

What Didn’t Happen: No Couping

Election interference spearheaded by the Trump DOJ in the weeks and months before the election was an unprecedented abuse of the powers of the federal government to undermine free and fair elections to try to preserve the power of the president’s party in Congress.

But it started to become apparent late last week that there was no master plan or strategy for Main Justice that went beyond a relatively meager effort to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting as a pretext for contesting California elections. But even that largely fell apart by Election Day. The separate effort to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska (where the other Dan Sullivan is on track to finish FOURTH) was its own particular weirdness.

What remained unknown was whether the White House had its own plan for more sweeping and direct election interference through sheer use of force. In the end, nothing along those lines materialized at all.

I ran through two different checklists on Monday of different levels of election interference to look for on Election Day and essentially none of that came to pass. The third act of the play — the post-election period — was ripe for Trump-driven chaos if there were a lot of close races and control of the House and/or Senate hung in the balance. The Democratic sweep took that off table.

America will always break your heart but then find a way to redeem herself.

There remains an enormous amount of work ahead. The immediate work is to contain Trump for two more years. That is essential work, and it won’t necessarily yield decisive, crowd-pleasing outcomes like impeachment or criminal convictions or other much-needed public forms of accountability. But that doesn’t mean it can’t be effective politically beneficial. Regardless, it is absolutely necessary.

Coming into the election, I thought containing Trump was the best we could hope for — and frankly that public expectations among Trump foes were too high for what could be done beyond that. Rebuilding and reforming would have to come after winning the White House in 2028.

But the Democratic gains at the state level open up new avenues to begin some of the forward-looking work sooner: starting to repair the colossal damage Trump has inflicted, rebuilding civil society, enlarging and enriching public life in America, reforming a weakened political system that Trump was able to exploit.

All of those efforts can start now at the state level and set the stage for what can happened federally if and when Democrats control the White House and congressional majorities. It’s a chance for a flourishing of new kind of politics, reforms, initiatives, and approaches. See what works and apply it nationally.

But … having a firm new grasp on the levers of power does not in itself fundamentally change America.

The ingredients that led to Trump all remain: a broken information ecosystem; a virtually unrestricted campaign finance system; unsustainable levels of economic inequality and wealth concentration; and an emptiness at the heart of American political life. Perhaps worst of all, one of the two major political parties has abandoned democracy.

After the disaster of Trump’s second election, I wrote that this is no longer merely a political problem but a cultural one. Politics can only do so much. The greatest danger in MAGA’s authoritarian impulses was its abuse of the power of government to dictate culture: white, Christian, native born, intolerant, militaristic, and male dominant. It was the most perverse possible response to the existential threats of climate change and AI.

Regaining power doesn’t reclaim culture, but it’s a heck of a start.

items.title: Trump Waylaid by Amazing Series of Court Setbacks on Election Eve
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
It has been the most extraordinary 24 hours of legal setbacks for President Trump since the start of his second term.

The past two years of Trump’s clashes with the federal judiciary have been building toward the ultimate test for Article III judges: Would they hold the line and protect the 2026 election against a proven lawless, coup-plotting, insurrectionist president who has relentlessly vilified and chronically defied the judicial branch?

The answer yesterday and deep into the night — even from the Roberts Court, which created this Constitution-rattling mess — was a resounding yes.

In a sweeping set of rulings from coast to coast and from district courts to the highest court, President Trump, his deeply compromised Justice Department, and his way-outside-of-its-lane Department of Homeland Security were blocked at nearly every turn from interfering in state-run federal elections.

It was as refreshing as it was resounding.

SCOTUS to Trump: Talk to the Hand

The Supreme Court — in a move for which legal experts could not immediately recall a precedent — unceremoniously smacked down a request from Trump Solicitor General D. John Sauer before it even heard from the opposing side. Sauer was seeking a Supreme Court order for California to sequester and not yet count mail-in ballots from a dubious list of 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters. The Trump DOJ had already lost in the same case twice at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals and once at the district court.

By the time it went to the Supreme Court, the DOJ’s list of 20,000 voters was so thoroughly discredited that the solicitor general could not bring himself to vouch to the Supreme Court for the reliability of the list. Earlier in the day, in a separate case in D.C., a Trump DOJ lawyer under tough questioning from a federal judge admitted that it was “fair to say” the 20,000-voter list had a “high error rate.” It was a damning admission with adverse implications for the Trump administration across all of the legal challenges to its pretextual campaign against the myth of rampant noncitizen voting.

It left the solicitor general exposed in front of the Supreme Court, where all he could do was meekly gesture to the 20,000-voter list in California as something he “understood” from other components of the DOJ to be accurate. Justice Kagan referred the solicitor general’s transparently insufficient application for an injunction pending appeal to the full Supreme Court, which didn’t even ask for a response from the other side before rejecting it, with no dissents. The refusal by the six-justice conservative majority to entertain the latest bad-faith nonsense from the Trump DOJ captured the tone of the day.

Snatching Victory From the Jaws of Defeat

Even when it looked like the Trump DOJ had scored one legitimate win in court last evening, it immediately lost again. A three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit overturned a lower court order that had kept the Trump DOJ from making further demands to sequester alleged noncitizen ballots and from threatening prosecution for counting those ballots. But within a couple of hours the full 9th Circuit agreed to rehear the case en banc and vacated panel’s decision. A Trump win evaporated before the ink had dried.

A quick side point on another 9th Circuit case: Even though the Trump DOJ appealed the dismissal of its lawless effort to block the certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, it has not yet sought an emergency order from the appeals court. I don’t know if that’s a concession exactly or reading the writing on the wall — or, as I suspect, a strategic decision to wait to see if the election is close enough to warrant continuing to pursue the case after poll close today. Stay tuned.

Our go-to election expert, Rick Hasen, summarizes Trump’s attack on free and fair midterm elections:

It is hard to convey to nonspecialists how unlawful DOJ’s attempts to intervene in the California tabulation process and Alaska election certification are. These are not close cases, where people of good faith can disagree. The Trump Administration has been trying to assert federal control over state and local election processes, despite a lack of congressional authorization, 250 years of practice, and plenty of adverse precedent.

Boasberg Provides the Perfect Bookend

Much of the court action yesterday was in D.C., where a flurry of election-related cases were heard on emergency bases. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson forced the above-mentioned DOJ admission that its alleged noncitizen voter lists were not reliable in a case brought by the union for election workers. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan barred DOJ and DHS from sending any more alleged noncitizen voter lists to state and local governments. U.S. District Judge Reggie Walton gave the Trump DOJ a Pyrrhic victory after it insisted it would not use armed federal agents as election monitors.

But it was Chief Judge James Boasberg who provided the perfect bookend to the last two years of rogue Trump attacks on the federal judiciary. It was Boasberg who was blatantly defied by the Trump administration during the unprecedented Alien Enemies Act deportation over one wild weekend in March 2025. It’s Boasberg who has been single-handedly pursuing a contempt of court inquiry into that defiance despite Trump appointees on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals slow-rolling and handcuffing him. It’s Boasberg who has come under sustained rhetorical attack from the Trump White House.

So it was poetic that Boasberg randomly wound up with two of the Trump election interference cases, and it was fitting that Boasberg flashed his independence by ruling against the Trump administration in one and for it in the other. Boasberg was convinced by an expert’s report that the Trump DOJ’s list of 20,000 noncitizen voter was not reliable and blocked it from demanding that California segregate the ballots of those who appear on the list.

But in the other case brought by the DSCC, DCCC, and DGS (among others), Boasberg ruled they lacked standing: “Even extraordinary merits questions cannot justify the extraordinary relief of a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order if those seeking it lack standing.” But he also noted that the relief granted in the other case offered “modest relief” in this case too.

The courts universally held firm yesterday after what can best be called an uneven performance over the first two years of Trump II. But the trend lines are clear: The Trump DOJ long ago exhausted any good will, benefit of the doubt, or presumption of regularity. In the long term, that’s a tragic loss of a public good, another way Trump is leaving the Justice Department in ruins. But in the short term, it’s a essential realization by federal judges that took long in coming.

The Harshest Judicial Rebuke of Them All

Despite everything that was going on in the election realm, the most searing rebuke from any judge not just yesterday but in the entire two years of Trump II came in the Broadview 6 case in Chicago.

The case arises from Trump’s mass deportation operation, where most of the DOJ’s good will and record of fair dealing has been squandered. Not satisfied with its impunity in Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration aggressively prosecuted protesters of its thuggery there. The Broadview 6 prosecutions quickly unraveled, but not before the Trump DOJ allegedly made false statements in court to the judge in the case.

U.S. District Judge April Perry was unstinting in putting the screws to the Trump DOJ in a new order that was quite frankly jaw-dropping to read. She was particularly harsh on the recent conduct of the DOJ’s No. 3 official Stan Woodward, who parachuted into the case late last week even as he was being taken to the woodshed by another federal judge in the D.C. golf course case.

Judge Perry also took note of a new wrongful termination lawsuit filed by the former head of the FBI’s Chicago office which contained an extremely damaging allegation against U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros. Throughout the case, Boutros and his office have insisted that they never had any outside communications about the Broadview 6 case with either the White House or Main Justice. In his lawsuit, Douglas DePodesta claims otherwise, alleging that Boutros did discuss the case with Main Justice higher ups, including during an Oct. 7, 2025 meeting in DePodesta’s office. Two days later, prosecutors under Boutros sought the first flawed indictment against the Broadview 6.

(Even as all this was going on in Chicago, a magistrate judge in D.C. handed the Trump DOJ another stinging defeat on Monday when he dismissed its retributive prosecution of two former FBI agents in a transparently political case brought the week before the election.)

The interplay between the election cases and the mass deportation cases yesterday felt a little like a fable. The repeated bad faith, extralegal conduct, poor professionalism, and lack of candor has been most prevalent in the mass deportation cases. It is where slowly but surely federal judges had the scales removed from their eyes as to what the Justice Department has become. It took a scarily long time for many judges to catch on, but they finally have — and in the nick of time, with a free and fair election hanging in the balance.

Now the question is whether judges continue to hold the line in the potential post-election chaos.

items.title: How to Assess the Election Day Risk of Trump’s Lawless Attack on the Midterms
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
How to Think About Election Day Threats

With the worst of Trump’s pre-election attacks on the midterms either failed or foundering, let’s turn to the next act in this saga: scenarios for election interference on Election Day itself.

Trump’s attack on free and fair elections has been persistent but also opportunistic, operating less from a master plan than a series of impulses and lurching efforts. That makes it hard to predict, though some telltale patterns do emerge.

While we don’t know what Trump or his DOJ and DHS may have in store for Election Day, it is when his attack could get its most ugly, with particular concerns around state-sanctioned violence. But that’s at one end of the spectrum and there’s a lot of other higher risk but lower impact possibilities for tomorrow.

None of this is intended be predictive. I just want to frame up for you what to be looking for and how to think about the Election Days threats. The risks exist along a continuum that includes everything from fairly normal Election Day complications to what might look like a coup.

The range of Election Day concerns is so broad that it’s helpful to divide them into two categories: (i) transitory scenarios that bear mostly on Election Day itself; and (ii) scenarios that are likely to carry over into the immediate post-election period, including those intended to set the stage for post-election challenges.

It’s not so much that one bucket is more serious than the other (although kinda, as you’ll see below) or that the impacts are more or less real. It’s just that the first bucket of scenarios are mostly one and done on Election Day, and the second bucket of scenarios will persist into the fractious post-election landscape between the polls closing and the state-by-state certifications of their elections.

Election Day scenarios that are likely to be short-lived include, in rough order from rare to more common:

  • denying or limiting access to polling places, including disrupting and impeding voting;

  • threatening and intimidating voters and election workers at polling places, vote-counting centers, and the offices of elections officials;

  • misusing law enforcement or federal agents, including ICE, to instill fear and cast a pall over the election;

  • disputes over poll opening and closing times; long lines at polling places; ballot shortages; ballot and voting machine errors and snafus.

(The last item above encompasses typically discrete issues that pop up around the country in every national election but which rarely impact election results. They often get widespread and frenzied news coverage in the morning and afternoon of Election Day, when the news is otherwise slow because campaigning is done and all there is to do is wait until the results start to come in.)

The defining element of the scenarios in this first bucket is that they largely abate once the polls close. It is common for these concerns to take on outsized significance for a few hours on Election Day and then vanish from the national discourse. But they carry the risk of mushrooming into something bigger, especially this year, such as being used as a pretext to take more dramatic direct action to intervene in the election.

One last point: If there is any kind of concerted, pre-planned, extralegal attempt by the Trump administration to use the powers of the federal government to intervene in the election while voting is underway, we might first detect it among the actions listed above. It may start ambiguously as a prelude to the more direct interventions below.

Bucket No. 2: The Big Uglies

The second bucket of Election Day scenarios contains the most egregious, over-the-top tools in the authoritarian tool chest. The risk of the worst of these actually coming to pass is the highest it’s been in any of our lifetimes, but it still remains a fairly low risk overall. The impact though would be devastating.

The Election Day interference that will persist into the post-election phase includes, in rough order of less likely to more likely:

  • destroying ballots or otherwise compromising election security and integrity, including by foreign actors;

  • direct intervention by law enforcement or federal agents, including ICE, in polling places, vote-counting centers, and the offices of elections officials;

  • detaining, arresting, or charging elections workers and officials;

  • seizing ballots, ballot boxes, voting machines, and tabulating equipment;

  • sequestering whole categories of already-cast ballots;

  • mass challenges of already-cast ballots;

  • widespread challenges of normal Election Day processes and procedures;

  • refusal of individual candidates to concede after clear election defeats;

  • refusal to concede the loss of the House or Senate despite decisive election results;

  • inventing new pretexts and reusing old ones to refuse to accept the results of the election overall.

The scenarios in the second bucket range from grossly unlawful to the kinds of election delegitimization and extreme gamesmanship that we’ve seen throughout the Trump era but which aren’t per se illegal. It may be difficult on Election Day itself to identify immediately which election challenges are reasonably legitimate under the law — and which are not. That will shake out in the post-election period, but we may get an initial glimpse of them before Election Day is over.

The dividing line between the two buckets of scenarios above is imperfect and in some instances could get pretty blurry pretty fast. The line between federal agents vaguely intimidating voters near polling places versus directly intervening at a polling place versus detaining election workers can be crossed in a cascading series of failures within minutes.

The astute reader will also note that late on Election Day, after the polls close, is by definition the post-election period. So things like disrupting the tabulating of the votes or seizing tabulating equipment late tomorrow night might not technically be an Election Day concern. Point taken. But for the purpose of broadly alerting you to what to look out for tomorrow I didn’t want to arbitrarily cut it off when polls close, especially with our time zone differences, which puts different parts of the country in different phases of Election Day.

I haven’t really entertained here the worst of the worst fears: that the 2024 election was the last free and fair election or that the military will be deployed. I don’t think those are realistic scenarios.

Even the worst of the scenarios I do list above I expect would happen sporadically and in specific jurisdictions where either the election is close or Trump wants to make a point of dominance and punishment. In other words, I think it will likely follow the patterns of the rest of the Trump II presidency.

If you’re looking for a gut check, here it is: I don’t expect the worst of the above scenarios to come to pass.

U.S. elections are too decentralized and the powers of the executive branch alone are too limited in state-run elections for the nightmare scenarios to be more than a fairly remote risk. But an erratic head of state with authoritarian impulses who has built a cult of personality within the ranks of federal officials, runs a supine Department of Justice directly from the White House, and has an overfunded DHS at his disposal remains a very real risk, especially considering how huge the potential downside is.

I am most concerned about extreme Republican gamesmanship pushing the legal and political envelope for months to deny winning Democrats a majority in the House or Senate. Under that scenario, the shenanigans would start on Election Day and persist into January and perhaps beyond.

Even the perfectly legal contest of the 2008 Senate election in Minnesota denied Senate Democrats a 60th vote for months until Al Franken was finally seated in July 2009. Think of it as GOP transgression on steroids, drawing on elements of the 2000 Florida recount, , Jan. 6, and the invasive federal immigration operations in blue cities.

While I’m most concerned about that scenario — which would be very on brand for Trump II Republicans — I still wouldn’t rate it as likely, largely because Republicans will need lots of plausibly close races to maximize chaos — and polling suggests a blue wave. Decisive Democratic victories are the best way to mitigate this risk — but it shouldn’t take a wave election for the rule of law to prevail. Alas, here we are.

For the latest developments on all these fronts and everything else about the election, I’d urge you to monitor TPM’s latest live blog.

items.title: Trump's Initial Attack on Free and Fair Midterms Has Been Effectively Thwarted
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Let me start by emphasizing that past returns are not at all indicative of future results.

With that said, the federal courts have held their own so far through the pre-election phase of the Trump administration’s attack on free and fair elections. There’s still time for the Supreme Court to engage in mischief before Election Day, but there’s not much time. And that’s really the key thing.

I’ve had my hair on fire about the federal interference in the California elections since the evening of Oct. 13 precisely because that was far enough out from the end of voting for real damage to be done — but not enough time to respond to mitigate that damage.

What we couldn’t know then, but which now seems likely, is that the Trump DOJ’s effort — to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen votingas a pretext to assert federal power to change states’ election processes and procedures — was going to be largely limited to California. It’s the only place the Trump DOJ has gone to court to try to force the segregation of alleged noncitizen ballots and delay their counting — and it has so far lost, and decisively so.

I still don’t understand why the administration focused on only one state or why that state was California. It’s possible this was just the last gasp of months of pre-election efforts by the Trump administration to skew the elections — or I’m just missing something that I will rue for a very long time. But in a series of district court wins and in two rulings by the 9th Circuit yesterday, the Trump administration’s interference in California has been confronted squarely.

Even a late intervention from the Supreme Court in the California case (and the Trump DOJ hasn’t gone there yet as of Saturday morning) would have much less on-the-ground impact now because mail-in ballots have continued to be processed in the two weeks since it went to court. Once they’re processed, they can’t be linked to a particular voter, so they cannot be set aside. The batch of actionable ballots that could be segregated — which, honestly, wasn’t that big to begin with — continues to shrink.

In short, the pro-democracy forces have nearly run out the clock on the worst of the pre-election interference attempts.

But the pre-election phase is only Act I of this three-act play.

Act II is Election Day itself, where all manner of mischief is possible in an intense 24 hours. The spread of early voting has helped to reduce the overall potential impact of Election Day sabotage, but there are still risks — and importantly, what happens on Election Day can set the stage for Act III.

Act III is everything that happens post-election, from tallying the votes to challenging ballots already cast to recounts and certifications and ultimately election contests. It’s where close elections can be won or lost.

The three acts aren’t entirely distinct. They overlap and play off of one another. Good legal strategies, whether offensive or defensive, try to set the stage in Act I for what will happen in Act III. What the Trump DOJ is doing in the Alaska Senate race right now — even though it’s inane — is an example of laying the groundwork during the pre-election phase for what could become post-election challenges if the race is close.

What made the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting especially dangerous is that it was designed to create a pretext for post-election legal and political arguments as to why certain categories of already-cast ballots and perhaps entire election results should somehow be voided or disregarded.

With two acts left to go, we’re by no means out of the woods yet. But Act I carried a particular risk that we’ve largely managed to dodge. Let’s talk about that next.

The pre-election legal wrangling of Act I is particularly important because it is the phase most likely to result in changes to election processes and procedures nationwide.

That was especially true given the Trump administration’s concerted effort to use the supposed threat of noncitizen voters to impose sweeping national impediments to voting, like interposing the U.S. Postal Service as a chokepoint for mail-in ballots or requiring election officials to set aside and not count mail-in ballots based on dubious lists of noncitizen voters.

Any wins in court on those fronts would have potentially affected voters everywhere. Even a single win in one court would have buttressed subsequent efforts to make the same on-the-fly changes to processes and procedures in additional jurisdictions.

Act I is different in that way. By the time you get to Acts II and III, the legal battles are being fought mostly on the margins: individual races that are close and where it’s worth contesting every single vote that has been cast. The constellation of tight races worth litigating in Act III is invariably smaller than the entire pre-election playing field was in Act I. So while Act III can determine the ultimate outcomes — who wins and who gets control of the House and Senate — the impact on voters everywhere is more circumscribed.

We’re just nearing the end of Act I, and there’s still a long way to go. But the big, ugly attempted intrusions by the Trump administration have so far been repelled. And, while I say this guardedly, there’s just not much time left for the administration to parlay any wins it does manage in court over the next 72 hours into dramatic nationwide changes on the ground before Election Day.

items.title: DOJ Election Interference Turns Into Raw Thuggery
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
I have the same mix of feelings that I did in the days leading up to Jan. 6, 2021: a queasy feeling that things are about to spiral out of control along with the recognition that it could end up just being a clown show.

The Justice Department’s corrupt, heavy-handed, intimidation tactics of issuing grand jury subpoenas to election officials in California while launching a wave of new election-related subpoenas in Alaska is a level of thuggery we haven’t seen before and a grave threat.

The only more direct and dramatic interference in free and fair elections would be blocking voter access to the polls, seizing ballots, and refusing to abide by the results of the election. Stay tuned, I guess?

And yet there remains an unmistakable clownish quality to the whole endeavor, such as Attorney General Todd Blanche personally charging four misdemeanor cases in Nevada for alleged noncitizen voting, presumably because the top federal prosecutor in the state is implicated in the Trump U.S. attorney scheme and was disqualified.

It is, as always, both/and.

Trump DOJ Ignores Judges Warning

In California, the Trump DOJ reportedly made the decision to target election officials themselves with a new round of grand jury subpoenas, Bloomberg reports:

Justice Department leadership directed top federal prosecutors in California to pursue criminal subpoenas of state and local officials regarding their roles administering allegedly illegal voting, according to two people familiar with the situation.

This is different from earlier grand jury subpoenas in recent weeks that were directed at obtaining voting records to prosecute alleged noncitizen voting. The new subpoenas are going directly to election officials who are in the midst of counting votes and managing an election.

The new subpoenas aren’t limited just to Los Angeles County: “All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation,” the AP reported.

The subpoenas come after acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to election officials in every California county earlier this month warning that they faced potential criminal prosecution for counting the ballots of alleged noncitizen voters — an unprecedented interpretation of federal criminal law.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, echoed those threats in court this week.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter warned from the bench Tuesday that DOJ’s threats against election officials needed to “cease immediately.”

In his order rejecting the Trump DOJ’s request that he order Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count alleged mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters, Judge Carter warned DOJ again: “The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop.”

The next day came with word of the new round of subpoenas.

Conflicting Reports on Timing of Subpoenas

Not all of the reporting is consistent as to when subpoenas were issued and served. But it appears that some subpoenas of election workers went out as early as last week.

“At least two employees of Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week for a proceeding scheduled for Nov. 4, on the morning after the election,” the NYT reported.

Three subpoenas to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder were sent Oct. 21 and 24, according to the AP, which obtained copies of them:

The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. … They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.

Those subpoenas predate the new wave of subpoenas that reportedly began yesterday in all four federal district in California.

Again, the focus of these latest subpoenas is different than a separate batch of prior subpoenas that focused on getting voting records in order to prosecute individual voters for allegedly being noncitizens. One such subpoena was received by Orange County election officials yesterday, adding to the confusion.

Grand jury subpoenas days before the election is intimidation enough, but there was at least one extra twist: “Federal marshals served one county employee at home, despite having already served that employee at the registrar’s office and issuing a notification of counsel, according to officials familiar with the incident,” the NYT reports.

“Threats and intimidation have no place in elections,” said Dean Logan, the top election official in Los Angeles County.

Wave of Subpoenas in Alaska

Further seizing on the NYT report that tied the candidacy of the Dan Sullivan to the Senate campaign of Mary Peltola, the Trump DOJ issued a wave of new subpoenas ostensibly to investigate what it claims is a conspiracy to deceive voters — but which is in reality a last-ditch effort to save a key incumbent Republican senator.

“Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by [Wednesday] evening, one of the officials said,” according to CNN, which reported that additional subpoenas were expected yesterday.

There had already been a quiet federal investigation of the Sullivan candidacy before the NYT story, with some grand jury subpoenas issued and witnesses interviewed, CNN reported:

The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks.

It seems clear now that the NYT report embarrassed officials at Main Justice since the newspaper story went farther than its own investigation had.

In a move I’ve never seen before, the Alaska U.S. attorney Michael Heyman “un-recused” himself from the case after the NYT report at the urging of Main Justice, CNN reported. Heyman had previously recused himself early in the probe because he was in discussions with Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski about being nominated for a federal judgeship.

The prosecutor-in-chief made clear his intentions soon after the NYT story broke: “I think they should be prosecuted,” President Trump said. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.”

Trump: Why Is MY Beak Dry?!?

Special Weekend Morning Memo

Keep an eye on your inbox for a special weekend edition of Morning Memo.

With the campaigns chugging to the finish line and Trump election interference in full swing, Morning Memo will bring you the latest. Stay tuned …

items.title: Trump Is on an Absurd Collision Course With Yet Another Federal Judge
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Trump DOJ’s No. 3 Official in the Hot Seat

A golf course in D.C. is the improbable venue for another significant Trump II showdown between the executive and judicial branches.

Unlike, say, the Alien Enemies Act, Abrego Garcia, and immigrant habeas cases, where the actions that precipitated the conflict between the Trump administration and federal judges were unmistakably serious deprivations of liberty, the East Potomac Golf Course case has layers of absurdism, which we’ll get into below.

My main reason for catching you up on this second-tier constitutional confrontation is to preview an important hearing in the case tomorrow, so that I can come back to this later without burdening you with a whole bunch of backstory.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had already ordered the Trump DOJ to show cause by yesterday why it should not be ordered to preserve all records in the case in what could only be interpreted as a prelude to her considering sanctions against government lawyers for allegedly misleading her. Reyes was particularly focused on the Trump DOJ’s failure to comply with her orders to provide sufficient notice of the surprise removal of hundreds of trees on the golf course over the Columbus Day weekend.

But now Judge Reyes has a new bone to pick with the Trump DOJ.

Judge Reyes has suspected that the mass tree removal over the holiday weekend was part of Trump’s plan to remake the historic golf course without congressional approval — but the administration and DOJ lawyers have denied it, repeatedly and emphatically.

Then on Tuesday, on her own, Judge Reyes took judicial notice of a new Truth Social post by President Trump, in which he declared that the golf course will be closing on Nov. 15, and demanded to know why the Trump DOJ had previously told her otherwise:

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told the Court on October 19 that “[w]ith regard to the November 15th date… there is no plan to close the course.” The Court ORDERS Defendants to clarify, as part of their response to the Court’s show-cause order from October 26, whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026. And, if so, how that can be reconciled with Associate AG Woodward’s representation to the Court.

In her order, Reyes also scheduled a “status hearing” for Friday and ordered Woodward — who represented Trump’s co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago case and Jan. 6 rioters — to appear at the hearing in person. The DOJ’s No. 3 personally handling cases is unheard of, let alone doing the president’s dirty work. Getting hauled into court for allegedly misleading a judge is beyond next level stuff.

Yesterday, in his response to the court order, Woodward conceded that there is a plan to close the golf course, but he did not reconcile his prior statements to the contrary:

The undersigned acknowledges the President has twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15. Accordingly, Interior, acting through counsel, is working to develop a plan to implement that direction and will provide this Court with notice pursuant to the Court’s October 26, 2026, Order.

That prompted another stern order from Judge Reyes ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, which she has now recast as a show cause hearing that is quite a bit broader than merely whether the Trump DOJ must preserve documents in the case:

The Court ORDERS the Government to come prepared to state at the hearing: (1) whether it continues to maintain that there is no final agency action; (2) the dates and times at which President Trump “twice directed Interior and the National Park Service to close the park by November 15”; … and (3) the first date “Interior, acting through counsel” began “working to develop a plan to implement that direction,” id. Associate Attorney General Woodward remains ORDERED to appear at the hearing in person. The Court FURTHER ORDERS the attendance of at least one counsel from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor with pre-existing experience on this case.

Shortly thereafter, Woodward provided the court-required detailed notice of the administration’s plan to shut down the vast majority of East Potomac Park, including the golf course, even though the renovation plan at issue will not have been approved yet on the administration’s own timetable.

The ostensible reason for closing the golf course before getting approval for the renovation is familiar: “significant safety hazards.” It’s similar to the pretext offered for the separate closure of the Kennedy Center, another D.C. public asset that Trump has tried to turn into a personal project. In this case, the public safety hazard is an allegedly “deteriorated sea wall that is currently crumbling into the Potomac River.”

All of this is to tee up tomorrow’s show cause hearing for you. It’s admittedly an odd sideshow in the last week before Election Day. But it wouldn’t be Trump lawlessness without a heaping dose of absurdity.

Trump DOJ Election Interference Watch

: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter late yesterday rejected the Trump DOJ’s request to force Los Angeles County to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizen voters. In a stirring opinion, Judge Carter repeatedly blasted the Trump administration’s interference in California’s election:

Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch. In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.

: The Trump DOJ seized on a NYT investigation that tied the campaign of Mary Peltola to a scheme to add a second Dan Sullivan to the ballot. In a new filing by DOJ No. 3 official Stan Woodward, he withdrew his prior opposition to the Peltola campaign and the DSCC intervening in the DOJ lawsuit to block certification of the Senate election. Instead, Woodward said DOJ would use expedited discovery in the case to investigate the alleged “sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters” and whether the Peltola campaign “attempted to deceive” the court. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen assesses the legal implications of this whole mess.

: Secretary of State Steve Hobbs told the Trump DOJ that its purported list of 400 alleged noncitizen voters contained actual U.S. citizens. In a letter, Hobbs said it would “irresponsible and illegal” to segregate and not yet count mail-in ballots from voters on the Trump DOJ list.

SPLC Reveals Its Theory of the Case Against It

The Southern Poverty Law Center has revealed in a new filing its theory of how the vindictive prosecution of it by the Trump administration came to be.

The civil rights group alleges that the Trump DOJ — which has zeroed in on the SPLC’s former program of using white supremacists as paid informants against other white supremacists — was able to flip the SPLC’s own longest-tenured informant into a government informant against the SPLC because he had failed to pay income taxes for 30 years.

The SPLC alleges that the flipped informant practically became a member of the prosecution team, with numerous meetings and 1,800 text messages between him and investigators over the last year. Identified in the filing as “F-9,” the informant also provided documents, reports, and four so-called “Intelligence Briefings” to investigators, the SPLC alleges:

To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them. F-9 admitted that he has a “house full of documents,” some of which he has referenced plans to “shred.”

The immediate purpose of the SPLC’s new filing was to obtain permission to subpoena the informant and obtain a court order for the informant to preserve the materials in his possession.

Quote of the Day: Transformers Edition

“The Arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats. It will be utilized as a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense.”—

items.title: The Trump DOJ’s OTHER Scheme to Interfere in the Midterm Elections
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The Retribution: Election Interference Edition

The Trump DOJ’s unprecedented moves to stop ballot-counting and election certification are its most direct interference in the midterms — but it’s also bootstrapping in its long-running scheme of retribution against Trump foes in service of partisan campaign narratives while voting is underway.

By timing prosecutions and overt investigative steps to maximize their pre-election impact, the Trump DOJ is not merely ignoring long-standing department policy about avoiding the public impression of election meddling. It’s actively abusing the powers of the federal government by using federal law enforcement for partisan ends. It’s happening broadly under the auspices of DOJ, but Department of Homeland Security law enforcement components are also involved.

I had intended to write about this dynamic this morning anyway, and then the NYT and WaPo each published versions of the same story. I’d recommend both of them. Here are the recent cases most directly tied to complementing and reinforcing Trump campaign rhetoric while voting is underway:

  • : The Trump DOJ tried to indict the star witness of the Jan. 6 Committee yesterday — exactly one week before Election Day — but was rebuffed by a D.C. grand jury.

  • 2 FBI agents in Hunter Biden case: The first inkling of the no-true bill in the Hutchinson case came during a raucous hearing on concerns about a highly politicized and problematic new prosecution of two FBI agents involved in the Hunter Biden investigation. The flimsy case was thrown together on orders from FBI Director Kash Patel and was perceived inside the bureau as a political “witch hunt,” a key FBI witness testified yesterday. The case was first charged on Friday.

  • : The Oct. 5 timing of Trump II’s criminal case against former FBI Director James Comey — which was unsealed this week at Comey’s request — seems to have been driven at least by an expiring statute of limitations, not solely the election. But they’re not mutually exclusive, of course. Like in the case against the FBI agents above, DOJ proceeded to file charges against Comey without a grand jury indictment.

  • : The Oct. 12 HSI raid on the private D.C. residence of a sitting Democratic member of Congress, who also is a Black woman of Somali heritage, managed to be brazen retribution and to mirror President Trump’s persistent racist targeting of Black women and Somali Americans.

  • Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D): On Oct. 14, the Trump DOJ indicted the President pro tempore of the Virginia Senate on allegations that her family set up an illegal marijuana business. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel held a press conference announcing the indictment.

  • : The FBI yesterday raided the Beverly Hill mansion of billionaire and former Democratic donor Stephen Cloobeck, reportedly a close associate of former Rep. Eric Swalwell. The NYT reports that the raid came as part of an ongoing investigation into sexual misconduct allegations.

The key is timing. Even where there might arguably be properly predicated investigations and prosecutions, the decision to proceed in high profile public ways before the election is a — notwithstanding Blanche’s feeble protests to the contrary.

A great visualization from the WaPo of the abuse of federal law enforcement in service of GOP election rhetoric around the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting:

Awaiting Ruling in CA Election Case …

As I reported late yesterday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter of Los Angeles said he will rule today on the Trump DOJ’s request for a TRO to segregate and not yet count ballots from a list of some 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters.

During a 3 1/2-hour hearing on the TRO, Judge Carter appeared likely to kick the core of the case past Election Day, thereby thwarting the Trump DOJ and minimizing the worst impacts of its effort to interfere in the election.

Bill Essayli Disqualified AGAIN

For the second time, a federal judge has found that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles. Essayli was slotted into the role as part of the broader Trump scheme to install loyalists as federal prosecutors in blue states, bypassing the Senate and defying federal law.

Essayli was previously disqualified by U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright of Hawaii from handling certain criminal cases as acting U.S. attorney because he overstayed his term in that role. Essayli was allowed to stay on as first assistant U.S. attorney and assumed all the duties of a regular U.S. attorney.

But subsequent appeals court decisions in others cases have more thoroughly blocked the workaround that President Trump and the DOJ used to install Essayli, so in a new ruling Judge Seabright tightened his previous decision even more. The most immediate impact will be to keep Essayli from managing or overseeing attorneys in the specific criminal cases where his appointment was challenged. Seabright gave Essayli a chance to appeal before the ruling goes into effect.

Ironically, Essayli personally argued the administration’s side in the California election case on the same day Seabright found him to be unlawfully serving.

The Ongoing Coverup of the Alex Pretti Killing

As Morning Memo first reported two weeks ago, despite what publicly looked like a breakthrough in July, the Trump administration has continued to stonewall Minnesota authorities trying to investigate the three ICE shootings during Operation Metro Surge.

Yesterday, the parents of Alex Pretti, one of the two U.S. citizens killed by ICE in January, held a press conference deploring the Trump DOJ’s conduct since the shooting of their son.

“Our son was murdered. We all saw it. And the lack of cooperation is baffling, it’s disappointing and reprehensible,” his father said.
